questions.question: How do Go packages and imports work?
questions.title: Packages And Imports
questions.direct_answer: A package is a directory of .go files sharing a package clause. Imports resolve to package paths (module-path + subdirectory). The package name (the clause) is what you call; the import path is how you find it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A package is a directory of .go files sharing a package clause. Imports resolve to package paths (module-path + subdirectory). The package name (the clause) is what you call; the import path is how you find it.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The mechanics, executed:

```go
// package example.com/mymod/db — the path
package db  // the package NAME — what callers say

func Query() { ... }
```

Importing:
```go
import "example.com/mymod/db"
// now: db.Query()
```

The two identities: the import PATH (example.com/mymod/db — module path + subdirectory, unique) and the package NAME (db — the package clause, what you reference). They usually match (the convention), but an import can alias: import mydb "example.com/mymod/db" — now mydb.Query().

The rules: one package clause per directory (all files in a dir are one package); the package name is the identifier (short, lowercase); imports are per-file (you import what each file uses); the main package is the binary entry point (func main).

The visibility coupling: imported = the package sees only EXPORTED identifiers (the topic's uppercase rule). The import itself must be USED — an unused import is a compile error (Go's strictness — no accidental dead imports).

The structure pattern:
```
mymod/
  go.mod
  main.go          (package main)
  users/           (package users)
    users.go
    users_test.go
  db/              (package db)
    postgres.go
```

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    M[module example.com/mymod] --> P1[package main]
    M --> P2[package users]
    M --> P3[package db]
    P1 -->|import path| P2
    P1 -->|import path| P3
    P2 -->|uses exported only| P3
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The import resolution: the path is module-path-relative — example.com/mymod/db means the db directory under the module root (example.com/mymod in go.mod). The go tool maps path → filesystem → the directory's package, loading its compiled form (or compiling it).

The cycle rule: package A imports B, B imports A — a compile error. Go has no cycle tolerance (unlike some languages). The fix is extraction: the shared dependency moves to C (A→C, B→C, no cycle). This shapes architecture: cycles indicate conflation — the extraction is the discipline that keeps packages single-purpose.

The _ and . imports: _ "pkg" — the blank import (for side effects: driver registrations like _ "modernc.org/sqlite" — the init runs, the name isn't used). . "pkg" — the dot import (everything in the current namespace — test-only, the practice from the earliest Go tests; now rare and frowned upon outside tests).

The vendor directory: the module-aware build can read dependencies from ./vendor instead of the cache — vendoring for hermetic builds. go mod vendor creates it; -mod=vendor uses it. The complete-module-in-your-repo approach for maximum reproducibility.
